title: Karmic tail 6-17-11 in the destiny matrix: “Wasted Talent”

seo.title: Karmic tail 6-17-11 “Wasted Talent”: meaning and working it through
seo.description: The 6-17-11 tail: why a gift waits years for “later”, how the Lovers, the Star and Justice close the circle, and what to do so the talent is not lost again.

short: 6-17-11 is the tail of a person who has a gift, and a habit of putting that gift off. The first number, 6 (the Lovers), is the entry to the script: the decision is made by the heart. The second, 17 (the Star), is the gift itself, around which everything revolves. The third, 11 (Justice), is the root task: to make your own decision about your work, give it a measure and carry it out, or the gift remains a promise. In the destiny matrix tradition this tail is called “Wasted Talent”, less often “Unrealised Talent”. It has one lesson: choose your own work yourself, and answer for that choice with deeds — every day, not only in hours of inspiration.

paragraphs: Each position of the tail does its own job, so the order matters: the same arcana in a different sequence would describe a different script.

paragraphs: The circle usually closes like this. A chance comes up to do your own thing: a university place, an offer, a free year or just a free evening. The entry fires: the heart makes the decision, but at that moment it asks not “what do I love?” but “what will I be loved for?” — by parents, a partner, colleagues, an audience. The gift does not disappear: the Star keeps shining from “someday” and promises that real life is still ahead. And the root task — to pass your own verdict on your work and carry it out — is put off along with it. A few years later a new fork comes, and once again the winner is whatever is safer and easier for the people close to you to understand.
The word “wasted” sounds like a verdict, though the tail’s mechanism is a quiet one. Nobody destroys the gift. It is simply not chosen, year after year.

sections.h2: A gift is not handed out on merit: what Waite says about talent
paragraphs: The most unexpected clue to this tail is hidden in the text of Justice itself. Explaining the eleventh card, Waite separates two orders. The first is **“the moral principle which deals unto every man according to his works”**. The second is spiritual election, about which, in his words, “we have no canon of criticism or ground of explanation”. The comparison he chooses for it is unexpected — the gifts of the poet: **“we have them or have not, and their presence is as much a mystery as their absence.”** And he concludes: “The law of Justice is not however involved by either alternative.”

For a tail about wasted talent this is the key idea. A gift is not handed out on merit and not taken away as a punishment. The mottoes of the Star, in Waite’s words, are “Waters of Life freely” and “Gifts of the Spirit”: the gift is given for nothing. The phrase cuts both ways — what is given for nothing can also come to nothing — and the 6-17-11 tail decides which of the two comes true. Justice at the root does not ask whether a person has talent. It looks at deeds: what has been done with what was given. Wasted talent, in this reading, is a gift that never became deeds.

The other meanings of the root fit the story too. In Waite’s divinatory list Justice is “Equity, rightness, probity, executive”. The last word, executive, names the power that carries decisions out: a decision counts as made when it is carried out. Wen gives the traditional interpretation of the card as “the presentation of a decision that needs to be made by the Seeker”, who is urged to make it “fairly, with impartiality, and with integrity”. And she compares Justice precisely with the Lovers. The Lovers, for her, is “about making an ethical decision that involves the Seeker”. Justice is about a decision that involves “others who matter to the Seeker”. The tail starts with the first and runs into the second. Choosing one’s work almost never concerns one person alone: parents, a partner and the family’s money all take part in it. So the root task of 6-17-11 is not heroics and not stubbornness, but an honest decision that takes into account both the people close to you and yourself — and is then carried out.

There is one more detail. In Waite’s description of the Star the word “measure” sounds twice: the figure gives “some part and measure of her priceless possession”, and gives it “in the measure that they can receive her influx”. Measure is the word of the scales. Even the light of this tail is given out by measure, and measure stands at its root.
Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the destiny matrix: linking these lines to the tail is our reading.

sections.h2: Three ways to lose a gift
paragraphs: The formula 6 + 11 = 17 gives three ways to end up without a star: to love but decide nothing; to decide without love; or to hand the decision about your work over to someone else’s court. Usually one script dominates in a person, but over a lifetime they can take turns.

The work is truly loved, but no decision about it is ever made. The person catches fire, buys paints, a course or a guitar, writes the first chapters — and stops at the point where the novelty has worn off and the mastery has not yet arrived. Unfinished work gets hidden: showing a draft seems scarier than not doing it at all. A couple of years later it all starts again with a different instrument, and the “when I have time” list grows longer. The Lovers are in place, the Star is shining — what is missing is the eleventh arcanum: a decision with a measure and a term, carried out even through the boring middle. Justice deals according to works, and the dreamer has only intentions.

paragraphs.h3: Justice without love: “the model student of someone else’s choice”

paragraphs: Here it is the other way round: there is plenty of duty, reliability and honesty, but they serve someone else’s choice. The choice was once made for the person, or they chose something “serious” themselves — a profession that was approved of, a path with predictable money. The arguments sound fair: the parents invested so much, the family needs a dependable income, this is the honest thing to do. The person conscientiously carries out this choice and often reaches a good result. Outside it is success; inside there is a feeling of living someone else’s correct life. In terms of Wen’s distinction, the decision about others outweighs the decision about oneself year after year: such a person is fair to everyone except themselves. The gift is filed under hobbies there is “no time” for, and the higher the achievements in the main job, the more expensive it seems to go back to it.

paragraphs.h3: A star for the audience: “light on demand”

paragraphs: The third script is trickier. The gift works, but its fuel is admiration and approval: here the entry 6 sounds like a thirst to be loved, and the scales of the root are handed to the audience. The person shines brightly while they are praised, and goes out at the first cold reaction. Criticism feels like a verdict and like love being withheld, so the work is dropped not when it isn’t going well but when the applause stops. Sometimes pride becomes the defence — “they didn’t understand me”, “they didn’t give me my due”, “I’m above this” — and growth stops at the level where the praise already comes. It is no accident that pride keeps turning up among the reasons the tradition gives for this tail: it is the same star, only it shines for the audience rather than because shining is what stars do. Such a star expects a reward for the gift itself, although the law of Justice, according to Waite, is not involved with the gift: it deals according to works.

In many destiny matrix calculators and in popular readings of this tail, 11 is Strength. This is not a mistake: the deck has two numberings. In the old Marseille order Justice is eighth and Strength (La Force in French decks) is eleventh. Waite swapped them “for reasons which satisfy myself” and added that “the variation carries nothing with it which will signify to the reader”. This article, like the whole site, numbers the arcana after Waite: 8 is Strength, 11 is Justice.

If your calculator has Strength at 11, the tail reads like this. The Star is made of the Lovers and Strength: talent is love for the work plus the effort that sustains that love. The root task is will, courage and gentle staying power; Waite stresses that the Strength card has “nothing to do with self-confidence in the ordinary sense”. In this reading the dreamer loses the gift for lack of patience, the model student because their strength is pulling someone else’s cart, and the main practice is a small daily quota instead of bursts.

paragraphs: The two readings agree on the main thing. In both the gift is lost in the middle of the road, and in both the way out is not a feat but a small regular measure. The difference is in what the person lacks. Whoever recognises themselves in “the dreamer” is closer to the question of Strength. Whoever recognises themselves in “the model student of someone else’s choice” is closer to the question of Justice: they have strength enough; what they lack is a decision of their own.

sections.h2: What the tradition says about the past incarnation
paragraphs: In the destiny matrix tradition a tail describes experience the soul brings from past incarnations. For 6-17-11 the story goes like this: the person had a bright gift — for art, for words, for a craft, for working with people — and gave it up. Different reasons are given:

ul: they chose security: the gift did not put food on the table, and family and obligations demanded a dependable income;
they got scared after a failure or mockery and decided not to take risks again;
they stopped out of pride: they won recognition and stopped growing;
they handed the gift over to others: parents, a teacher or a patron controlled it, not the person themselves.

paragraphs: In this life, by the same logic, the gift comes back together with the old choice — and with the old temptation to put it off.

If the idea of rebirth does not appeal to you, read this part as a description of a repeating script. It is tested by observation, not by faith. Recall two or three forks in the road where you could have chosen your own work. If every time “safer”, “later” or “what will people say” won, the tail describes you exactly. The same plot is worth looking for in family stories: who in the family “could have become…” but didn’t.

sections.h2: How the tail shows up in life
paragraphs: It often starts early: the child has an activity they can lose themselves in for hours without being reminded. After that there are two possible turns. The adults call the activity frivolous and steer the child towards something that “will come in handy”. Or they praise so warmly, and so much for being “talented”, that the child begins to fear turning out untalented and quits at the first difficulty. The paths differ, the result is the same: the decision about the gift is not made by the child.

The eleventh arcanum gives this tail reliability: a person with 6-17-11 honestly carries out whatever they have taken on, and that is the trap. They can achieve a lot in work they did not choose out of love, and it is precisely success that makes returning to the gift ever more expensive: why take a risk when everything is fine as it is? The phrase “you can’t make a living from creative work” sounds especially convincing here, because real achievements in another field stand behind it.

The way out is rarely to drop everything one day. This tail is worked through with measure and consistency, not with a leap: the gift grows alongside the main job — first it gets a few hours a week, then its first clients or students, then an income of its own. The first money for your own work matters not for its amount. For Justice it is a fair exchange: the gift acquires a price, and the activity stops being a pastime and becomes work you can defend to yourself and the people close to you.

Here the tail has a feature you can see right on the diagram. Point M, where it starts, also opens the relationship line (M–R1–R). For everyone who has 6-17-11, the entry into closeness is the Lovers too. So for this tail the question “love or the gift?” is not a metaphor: both roads start from the same point of choice.

In life this looks different from person to person. The gift is put off “for the family’s sake” — and then quietly charged to the family’s account. A dependable partner is chosen for whom the passion is a whim. Or the partner is cast as an audience and expected to provide admiration instead of closeness. It is good to have someone beside you who asks “how is it going?” and wants to see what you have made. It is bad when the partner is given the role of judge, and whether to carry on starts to depend on their verdict. The root of this tail is Justice, and the judge’s seat in it stays with the person themselves: listening to the people close to you is right and necessary, but the decision about your work is yours, made honestly and with regard for those it affects.

sections.h2: What else is always in a chart with this tail
paragraphs: The matrix formula ties the tail rigidly to other points, so everyone who has 6-17-11 shares a few more things. This was checked by running all dates from 1900 to 2099.

paragraphs: A separate word about the centre. Both 13 and 22 are energies of beginning: Death easily ends and renews, the Fool easily starts and dislikes commitment. The root task of the tail, Justice, demands the opposite — a commitment carried out to the end of its term, and judgement by what has been done rather than by what has been started. Hence an observation worth testing on yourself: starting over feels familiar and calm to a person with 6-17-11, and the hardest part is the middle of the road, where there is neither novelty nor result. That is exactly where the gift is most often lost. But the same ease has its use too: closing off a path that was never theirs is easier for such people than for many others.
The tail is most likely about you if you recognise at least three points out of nine:

ul: In childhood you had an activity that made you forget the time, and it was called frivolous early on — or you dropped it yourself when it got hard.
You have a “when I have time” list, and it is already several years old.
You start new things easily and rarely get to a level you can be proud of.
Showing unfinished work is scarier than not doing it at all.
The sharpest sting is envy of people who openly do “your” work, even if they do it worse.
Praise embarrasses you, and criticism switches off the wish to carry on.
You check decisions about your work against the reactions of the people close to you before you check them against your own wishes.
You keep your promises to others, and put off your promises to yourself year after year.
At work you are reliable and conscientious, but you can’t remember when it last gave you joy.

sections.h2: How to work through the 6-17-11 tail
paragraphs: The work goes through the same three points, only this time the circle is walked consciously: acknowledge the gift, choose it yourself and carry out the decision.

ol: **Name the gift.** It rarely hides — it simply goes unacknowledged. Three reliable sources: what you did as a child without being reminded; what people ask you for, assuming it costs you nothing; whom you envy. For this tail envy works like a compass: it points not at something belonging to others but at something of your own that you left behind.

**Catch the moment of choice.** The entry 6 fires at the moment of decision, so that is exactly where the questions need to be asked. “Am I choosing this because I love it — or because this is how I’ll be loved?” “Is this my choice, or someone else’s that I long ago mistook for mine?” The answer does not have to be heroic. It has to be honest.

**Measure out the gift’s share.** Justice holds the scales, and the first decision is about measure: how many hours a week, how much money, for what term. Not everything and not nothing, not bursts and not feats, but a small quota that is impossible not to meet. Twenty minutes, a page, one sketch. A decision about the gift counts as made when it is carried out — it is no accident that Waite’s list of meanings for Justice includes “executive”. Count the days, not the results.

**Decide about “quitting” in advance.** The trial period is set before you start — say, three months — and until it ends the question “should I go on?” is not up for discussion. The verdict is passed at the end of the term, not in the middle of the hearing. That way the middle of the road, the most dangerous place for this tail, stops being a place for decisions.

**Let the water flow.** On the Star card in Waite’s deck a young woman pours water from two ewers — onto the land and into the pool — and the mottoes of the card, in Waite’s words, are “Waters of Life freely” and “Gifts of the Spirit”. A gift hoarded until it is perfect stops being a gift. Show what you have made regularly, starting with a safe circle: one person, then a few, then the public.

**Judge by deeds, not by talent.** The question “do I have talent?” has no answer: for Waite the gift of the poet is as much a mystery in its presence as in its absence, and the law of Justice is not involved with it. Justice asks something else — what has been done this week. Compare your draft with your own previous draft, not with someone else’s finished work. Among the reversed meanings of Justice Waite lists “bias” and “excessive severity” — and this tail often judges itself in just that way. Look at the last time you dropped something: what was decisive — fear of judgement, boredom, resentment at being misunderstood, or a pride that will not let you be a beginner? An honest answer is not an accusation but information for the next decision.

**Agree with the people close to you out loud.** If the gift needs time that now belongs to the family, the decision is discussed, not made into a silent sacrifice. The gift can be put off — honestly, for a set term and with an explanation, not “for your sake” only to present the bill later. Wen writes of Justice: “What is fair will feel fair.” A silent sacrifice does not feel fair — neither to the one who made it nor to those it was made for.

**Don’t burn your bridges.** With a centre of 13 or 22 the temptation to drop everything and start a new life on Monday is strong. It does not help this tail: the tail is worked through with measure and consistency, not with a leap. A fair decision takes into account both the gift and your current life: let the gift grow alongside that life until it is strong enough to take up more room in it.

sections.h2: Signs that the tail is being worked through

ul: The gift has a place in your schedule, not only in your dreams.
You can show a draft, and it is not a disaster.
Criticism upsets you but does not stop you.
You keep your promises to yourself as you keep your promises to others.
You have agreed out loud with the people close to you on time for your work, and nobody is keeping a secret bill.
Envy has turned into curiosity: you want to know how someone else’s work is set up.
Someone starts learning from you, or asks you for exactly your kind of work.

paragraphs: A mature 6-17-11 is a person who shines without permission and without applause. They have decided for themselves what their gift serves, and they answer for what has been done with it. Their gift no longer depends on whether they are loved for it, and so it goes generously to others.
Parents can do more here than it seems: the childhood script of this tail takes shape with their involvement.

ul: **Don’t choose something “serious” for the child.** You can advise and explain, but let the last word about the work they love stay with them — that is their entry 6. The right to decide also teaches them to answer for the decision.

**Praise regularity and what has been done, not “talent”.** Praising talent teaches a child to count on the Star. Praising what has been done teaches the main law of this tail — to judge yourself by deeds.
**Don’t make love a reward for performances.** A child with this tail quickly learns that they are loved for success, and starts to be afraid of trying.

**Allow them to quit, but not at the first plateau.** Agree on a term in advance: until the end of the season, until the end-of-year concert. An agreement that both sides keep is the first lesson of Justice.

sections.h2: How to find the tail in your matrix
paragraphs: The tail sits on the bottom ray of the matrix. **D** is the bottom point: the sum of the arcana of the day, month and year of birth (numbers over 22 are reduced by adding their digits). **E** is the centre: the sum of the day, month, year and D. **M** is the point between D and the centre, D + E. **N** is the point between D and M, D + M. The tail is written from the inner point to the outer one: M–N–D.

An example for 22.06.1990. The day is 22, the month 6, the year 1 + 9 + 9 + 0 = 19. D = 22 + 6 + 19 = 47 → 4 + 7 = **11**. E = 47 + 11 = 58 → 5 + 8 = 13. M = 11 + 13 = 24 → 2 + 4 = **6**. N = 11 + 6 = **17**. The tail is 6-17-11. Gender plays no part in the calculation.

sections.h2: What this article is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the destiny matrix scheme with points D, E, M and N described above; sums over 22 are reduced by adding their digits. The fixed numbers in a chart with this tail and its frequency were found by running all dates from 1900 to 2099.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, 1922 reprint) and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Quotations are given in the authors’ original wording. Numbering follows Waite: VIII is Strength, XI is Justice.

**The name “Wasted Talent” and the past-life legend** come from popular interpretations of the destiny matrix. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails: assembling the three cards into a script and reading the two numberings is the author’s interpretation.
This is an esoteric model for self-observation, not a forecast of events.

faq.a: Yes. It is one triad written from different ends: read from the bottom up, from D to M, you get 11-17-6. In the M–N–D order the combination 11-17-6 never comes up for any date: by the formula the first number of a tail is always a multiple of three — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21 — and 11 is not divisible by three.

faq.q: Why is 11 Strength in one calculator and Justice in another?
faq.a: These are two numberings of the deck. In the old Marseille order and in most destiny matrix calculators the eighth card is Justice and the eleventh is Strength. Waite swapped them, and in his deck the eleventh is Justice; this article and the whole site follow him. The tail does not change: the numbers are the same, only the name of the root changes. How 6-17-11 reads with Strength at the root is covered in the section “Two numberings”.

faq.q: Does the tail mean that I have a talent? What kind?
faq.a: The tail is about how you treat a gift, not about its size or field. It comes up for roughly one person in twenty-three, so it is not a certificate of genius. Nor does the root of the tail measure the gift: Waite writes of the gifts of the poet that “we have them or have not”, and the law of Justice is not involved with them — it looks at works. Look for the field in the personal talent line of your matrix (B–P–K), in what you did as a child, and in what other people ask you for.

faq.q: I’m over forty. Is it too late?
faq.a: The tail sets no deadlines. It describes a choice that repeats, which means the chance to choose differently repeats too. With age a gift often changes form: someone who did not become a musician can teach, arrange, or write about music. The tradition singles out the dangerous version for the second half of life: the postponed dream is handed down to the children, and they are expected to fulfil it. A child will not light your star for you, and their own goes out because of it.

There are no bad tails. 6-17-11 does not predict events and does not claim that nothing will work out for you. It shows where the link between love and decision usually breaks. When both are in place, the same triad describes a person around whom others want to create their own things too: the Star gives light, the Lovers make it warm, Justice makes it honest and well measured.

faq.q: I found 6-17-11 not in the tail but elsewhere in my chart
faq.a: The same numbers in another position — the money line, the relationship line, the talent line or a program — are read according to their role, and this article does not apply to them: it is only about the bottom ray M–N–D. If the triad comes up in a compatibility matrix, it describes the couple’s shared chart, not your personal script.

intro: The key to the tail is hidden in its arithmetic. The middle number is the sum of the two outer ones: **6 + 11 = 17**. Here the Star is literally made of the Lovers and Justice: in this triad talent equals love for the work plus a decision that carries that love out — gives it time, a place and a term. Take away either term, and there will be no star. Almost everything that happens to people with this tail is explained by which of the two terms has dropped out for them.

If the calculator showed you 11-17-6, it is the same tail read from the bottom up. And if your calculator calls 11 Strength, it is this tail too: the deck has two numberings, and both readings are covered below, in the section “Two numberings”.

The second is election, about which “we have no canon of criticism or ground of explanation”, like the gifts of the poet: **“we have them or have not, and their presence is as much a mystery as their absence.”** “The law of Justice,” Waite concludes, “is not however involved by either alternative.”

The tradition explains the name with a legend about a past incarnation: the person had a bright gift and gave it up — chose security, took fright at mockery, stopped out of pride, or handed the gift over to others. In this life the gift supposedly comes back together with the old temptation to put it off.

Believing in rebirth is not required: the script shows in the forks in the road where one’s own work could have been chosen, and in what won at each of them — “safer”, “later” or “what will people say”. But the key to the name lies not in the legend but in the cards.

report.h3: Given for nothing, or come to nothing

report.h3: The heart asks “what will I be loved for?” instead of “what do I love?”

report: A chance comes up to do one’s own thing: a university place, an offer, or just a free evening. The tail’s entry, the Lovers, fires — the heart makes the decision. But it asks “what will I be loved for?” — by parents, a partner, colleagues, an audience. The Star shines from “someday”, and the root task — to pass one’s own verdict on one’s work and carry it out — is put off along with the gift. **Nobody destroys the gift. report.h3: Three ways to end up starless

The model student of someone else’s choice decides, but without love. There is plenty of duty and honesty, but they serve someone else’s choice: the parents invested so much, the family needs a dependable income, this is the honest thing to do. Outside it is success; inside, the feeling of living someone else’s correct life. Such a person is fair to everyone except themselves, and the higher the achievements, the more expensive a return to the gift seems.

The third way is trickier: handing the scales to the audience. The person shines brightly while they are praised and goes out at the first cold reaction. The work is dropped not when it isn’t going well but when the applause stops. It is no accident that pride keeps turning up among the reasons the tradition gives for this tail: it is the same star, only it shines for the audience.

Justice demands the opposite — a commitment carried out to the end of its term. report.h3: The verdict comes at the end of the term, not in the middle of the hearing

report: The way out begins with naming the gift. It rarely hides — it simply goes unacknowledged: what was done in childhood without reminders, what other people ask for, assuming it costs nothing, whose work stirs envy. For this tail envy works like a compass: it points not at something belonging to others but at something of one’s own that was left behind.

Next, measure out the gift’s share. Justice holds the scales, and the first decision is about measure: how many hours a week, how much money, for what term. Not feats, but a small quota that is impossible not to meet: twenty minutes, a page, one sketch. Set the trial period in advance — say, three months — and do not discuss whether to go on until it ends.

Judge by deeds, not by talent: the question “do I have talent?” has no answer, while the question “what has been done this week?” does. And if the gift needs time that now belongs to the family, the decision is discussed out loud. Wen writes of Justice: “What is fair will feel fair.” A silent sacrifice does not feel fair — neither to the one who made it nor to those it was made for.

report.h3: A light that needs no applause

report: **A gift hoarded until it is perfect stops being a gift.** The work is shown regularly, starting with a safe circle: one person, then a few, then the public. Bridges are not burned: the gift grows alongside the main job until it brings in its first money. That money matters not for its amount: for Justice it is a fair exchange, and the gift acquires a price.

A mature 6-17-11 is a person who shines without permission and without applause. They have decided for themselves what their gift serves, and they answer for what has been done with it. The Star gives light, the Lovers make it warm, Justice makes it honest and well measured.
